paragraphs.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is a syndrome of endocrine and nonendocrine tumors caused by germline pathogenic variants or genomic rearrangements of the MAX gene (Haider et al., 2025). Its main feature is highly penetrant pheochromocytoma, often bilateral and sometimes metastatic, with or without paraganglioma (Maggacis et al., 2026). Other reported tumors include pituitary neuroendocrine tumors that secrete growth hormone and/or prolactin, other neural crest-derived tumors such as ganglioneuroma and neuroblastoma, and possibly parathyroid adenomas and nonendocrine tumors (Seabrook et al., 2021; Lian et al., 2024; Maggacis et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) updated their report of a family with pheochromocytoma over 3 generations. The proband had neuroblastoma of the broad ligament at 17 months of age. At age 22 years she developed a right pheochromocytoma, a ganglioneuroma at the site of the original neuroblastoma, and an ileal schwannoma. Six years later she had a left pheochromocytoma with a mature ganglioneuroma, and a leiomyosarcoma of the mesosigmoid was removed at the same time. She later developed cutaneous and other metastases of the leiomyosarcoma, a hepatic carcinoma at 42 years, and a uterine leiomyoma. Her paternal grandfather had bilateral pheochromocytoma at 70 years. Her youngest brother presented at 31 years with cardiomyopathy complicated by Takotsubo syndrome, which led to the diagnosis of bilateral pheochromocytoma. Her paternal uncle was found at 56 years to have a clinically silent 11-mm right adrenal nodule with strong [18F]-DOPA uptake. Her father had lung adenocarcinoma at 47 years and prostate cancer at 54 years but no evidence of pheochromocytoma.

paragraphs.text: Seabrook et al. (2021) reported 2 families with germline MAX variants who were studied at university hospitals in Australia. Family A included several individuals with pheochromocytoma, some bilateral and some metastatic. Two children in the family, without pheochromocytoma to date, had neuroendocrine tumors: a paravertebral ganglioneuroma in one and an abdominal neuroblastoma in the other. One individual had acromegaly, and immunohistochemistry of that patient's pheochromocytoma tissue was positive for growth hormone-releasing hormone. Another individual with previously resected pheochromocytomas had pituitary enlargement and elevated IGF1. In family B, the proband had bilateral and metastatic pheochromocytoma, a prolactin-producing pituitary tumor, multigland parathyroid adenomas, chondrosarcoma, and multifocal pulmonary adenocarcinomas.

paragraphs.text: Lian et al. (2024) investigated 19 individuals from 3 families with pheochromocytoma. Six carried germline MAX variants, and 3 of these had pheochromocytoma. The proband of family A was a man diagnosed with right pheochromocytoma at 24 years after more than 2 years of high blood pressure (200/110 mm Hg at presentation). At 36 years a left adrenal mass was found, with plasma norepinephrine raised to 2,766.00 ng/L, and he was diagnosed with metachronous bilateral pheochromocytoma. The proband of family B, a 34-year-old man, had asymptomatic bilateral adrenal masses with normal plasma catecholamines and metanephrines; pathology confirmed bilateral pheochromocytoma. The proband of family C, a 64-year-old woman with occasional paroxysmal headache, had a right pheochromocytoma with raised plasma norepinephrine. The 3 carriers without disease, aged 13, 59, and 43 years, had no evidence of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma, pituitary adenoma, or other neuroendocrine tumors.

paragraphs.text: Lian et al. (2024) also reviewed 109 patients with germline MAX mutations from 87 families, comprising their 6 carriers and 103 carriers from 84 previously reported families. Of the 109 patients, 101 (92.7%) developed pheochromocytoma. The mean age at diagnosis was 32.8 +/- 12.6 years (range, 13-80), and the male-to-female ratio was 1.3:1. Fifty-nine patients (58.4%) had bilateral pheochromocytoma (47 simultaneous, 12 metachronous), and 19 (18.8%) had metastatic pheochromocytoma. Eleven (10.9%) also had chest or abdominal paraganglioma, and 1 had only head and neck paraganglioma. Nine patients (8.3%) had pituitary neuroendocrine tumors: 3 with raised growth hormone only, 4 with raised prolactin only, and 1 with both. Eleven had other neuroendocrine tumors diagnosed between ages 0.7 and 60 years, including 4 with primary hyperparathyroidism. Seven (6.4%) had non-neuroendocrine tumors, and 3 carriers were asymptomatic. Of the 87 families, 22 (25.3%) had a family history of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma.

paragraphs.text: In a systematic review, Charoenngam et al. (2026) identified 45 studies covering 127 patients with germline MAX mutations. The median age at first tumor diagnosis was 29 years (interquartile range 23.0-39.0), and 37.0% of patients were women. The most frequent tumors were pheochromocytoma (112 patients), pituitary adenoma (11), and paraganglioma (10), with median ages at diagnosis of 31.0, 33.0, and 43.0 years, respectively. Of the pheochromocytomas, 38.3% were unilateral and 27.6% were metastatic, and most secreted norepinephrine. The authors considered the causal association between primary hyperparathyroidism and MAX loss to be uncertain.

paragraphs.text: In the family reported by Cardot Bauters et al. (2020), the brother of the proband developed bilateral pheochromocytoma but did not carry the familial KIF1B variant. A gene panel identified a heterozygous c.145T-C transition in the MAX gene, resulting in a ser49-to-pro (S49P) substitution (see Ser49Pro under Allelic Variants). By ACMG criteria the variant was classified as of uncertain significance. However, both of the brother's tumors had lost the wildtype MAX allele, and structural modeling predicted that the variant was deleterious. The proband, her father, her grandfather, and her paternal uncle were also heterozygous for the variant. No loss of the wildtype MAX allele or second somatic MAX mutation was found in the proband's pheochromocytomas. The authors noted that a high proportion of normal tissue in the samples could not be ruled out as a cause. Exome sequencing of the proband excluded pathogenic variants in other pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma genes and in 30 cancer-predisposition genes.

agent.process_note: I read all 12 files in full. Three are full texts (Cardot Bauters 2020, Lian 2024, Maggacis 2026), eight are abstracts only, and Casey 2025 is a title-only author correction, which I left uncited. I used Grep to check the pedigree labels in Cardot Bauters, whose text labels the proband's father inconsistently (II-1 vs II-2), so I avoided labels. No MIM number for MAX was supplied in the reference data, so the intro gives none; I took the chromosome location (14q23.3) from Lian 2024 and Maggacis 2026. The R33X mutation is described only through reviews (Lian 2024, Maggacis 2026) and has no primary report in the folder, so I did not create an allelic variant for it. Details of the 2011 MAX mutations, and the cases in Taieb 2018, were not available beyond the abstracts. Ancestry was not stated for any family. The reports disagree on catecholamine phenotype (mainly norepinephrine vs mixed) and on metastasis rate (18.8% vs 27.6%), and the entry reports both.
